newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Kulikov slams Trans-World in aluminium row.
newsitem.headline: Russian Kulikov slams Trans-World in aluminium row.

text.p: Russian Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov slammed international metals firm Trans-World Group on Tuesday for complaining of mistreatment in the aluminium sector, but said it would not confiscate property.

Kulikov, in an acerbic letter to Trans-World executive chairman David Reuben, vowed to continue an investigation into alleged crimes in the sector, which he said had given foreign firms an unfair advantage in the key metals sector.
Kulikov said he was responding to full-page advertisements run by Reuben in major international newspapers last week which criticised Moscow for harassing the company.
Reuben has said previously his firm is completely above board.

"A strong state ensures honest competition between domestic and foreign producers by means of offering them possibilities for fair competition," Kulikov wrote in the letter, a copy of which was faxed to Reuters by the Interior Ministry.
"Mr Reuben, it cannot be unknown to you that at present, such equal possibilities in the Russian aluminium sector do not exist."
But Kulikov said Reuben's fears that Moscow was seeking to renationalise domestic aluminium enterprises -- where Trans-World has equity stakes -- were misguided.
"You must understand that your accusations do not correspond to reality and, consequently, are at the very least misguided.

"Today's Russia is a little different from the one to which your little-known firm came five years ago. Today, no one would even put it into his head to doubt the steadfastness of the institution of private property," Kulikov wrote.

The bitter, public row between Moscow and London-based Trans-World -- a private commodities powerhouse -- has raised questions over whether Russian supplies of primary aluminium to world markets might be jeopardised.
Kulikov said he did not understand Reuben's objections to the probe since, he said, Reuben was broadly insisting on fair play for all foreign investors in Russia.

"Mafia-structures are monopolising the market, destroying it, turning economic relationships into relationships between criminal syndicates," Kulikov said, vowing to press on with his fight against crime and to ferret out corruption.
"Big capital does not want to have anything to do with dirty money or with dirty people."
The Prosecutor-General's press office, quoted by Interfax news agency, said on Friday it was activating a probe started by the Interior Ministry into possible crimes in the aluminium sector.
Kulikov said last month that domestic aluminium plants needed protection from Western firms and that imports of raw materials to make metal, predominantly alumina, should carry tariffs.

Kulikov, repeating the protectionist rhetoric, said in his letter that companies supplying alumina to Russian smelters had an unfair advantage because they did not have to pay a 20 percent value-added tax.

"I consider it useful to remind you that the competitive advantage which foreign companies have on the Russian market are dooming it to poverty and depriving tens of thousands of Russian citizens in the alumina industry," Kulikov wrote.
Russia accounted for a major portion of world primary aluminium exports last year, delivering 2.44 million tonnes to markets out of total output of 2.87 million.
